title: Interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality: a global systematic review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Perinatal suicidality (suicidal thoughts, behaviours, plans and attempts) is a risk factor for suicide. Evidence on interventions to reduce perinatal suicidality remains limited. This systematic review examined the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions to reduce suicidality in perinatal women.
METHODS: This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251081528). Seven databases were searched from 2010 to December 2025. Interventions assessing a reduction in perinatal suicidality as a primary, secondary, or safety monitoring outcome were included. Two reviewers independently screened articles. A narrative summary was compiled. Risk of bias was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.
RESULTS: Six studies were included: 5 randomised controlled trials (3 individually randomised, 1 cluster, 1 noninferiority) and 1 historical controlled trial. Three studies investigated suicidality as a primary or secondary outcome, and three studies collected suicidality data for safety monitoring. Of these, two investigated multidisciplinary community health programmes, and one evaluated a behavioural activation therapy. Two studies showed a reduction in suicidality, and one showed a significant reduction at 3-4 months postpartum, but not at 7-8 months. Three studies assessed suicidality as safety monitoring. These studies investigated eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy, a practice-level intervention incorporated into obstetric practices, and an electronic mindfulness-based intervention. These studies were not adequately powered to assess a reduction in suicidality.
DISCUSSION: Few studies have investigated suicidality as a primary or secondary outcome. Although some health system level and psychological interventions were associated with a reduction in suicidality, robust evidence from interventions specifically designed to reduce perinatal suicidality is needed.
